Jeremy Hurtt woke up that winter morning in 2014, and after staring at the ceiling for a few minutes, headed out for a run, thinking it may be his last.
He headed toward the spot where the run—and everything else—could end. An overpass above an interstate in the town of Benton, Arkansas, a mile from the house he had been crashing in for the past few weeks, sleeping on a cold floor, getting by on the generosity of a friend. Money had troubled Jeremy for years. He did odd jobs around town for a few bucks, but mostly was bumming $10 and $20 from friends just to get by. He was 34 years old, with nothing in the bank, no home, no car, not even a driver’s license. All these little indignities, piling up, had started to bury him.
And then there were the memories, too.
Since finishing a deployment in Iraq in 2008, there’d been lots of days when Jeremy felt down, depressed—and seemed different from the playful, clownish, upbeat guy his Army pals and others had come to know. “He was no longer good-time Jeremy,” one friend says. “He was withdrawn, reclusive.” But he never seriously thought about hurting himself. Until that morning when the indignities were too many, and his mind couldn’t stop wondering why he was still alive and better people weren’t.
The overpass was a destination he had crossed before. On walks and runs when he was up for it. At that early-morning hour, semitrucks would be rushing below. He, on the other hand, wasn’t rushing, running at his usual 8-to-9-minute pace, which let his mind race ahead. Running was something he had done occasionally, a means to an end after his return home from Iraq, a way to stay somewhat fit. That morning, running was the means to get where he needed to go.
He thought of what would happen if he decided to jump. About the driver whose vehicle would likely strike him once he landed on the road. He didn’t want to cause another person pain. He knew from his time in Iraq the pain that comes with sudden death. But even this good intention couldn’t deter him from running ahead.
He gave little thought to what might happen if he didn’t jump.
He neared the overpass. A short way to go. The sound of semis intensified. Just a little farther. A railing on the overpass to climb over. The poor driver. One more step.
And then he heard something else. Words in his head.
Charlie-Mike.
If you’ve been in the military, you know Charlie-Mike. You may have heard the call, the command. Jeremy followed it often when stationed in Iraq in the mid–to-late aughts. It was a time when improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and explosively formed penetrators (EFPs) got mentioned on the nightly news as often as sports scores and tomorrow’s forecast. When American troops tried to end chaos in a country exacerbated by American miscalculation.
Charlie-Mike is military code: Continue the Mission. Move forward. In the face of adversity. No matter what.

Wells Fargo is no longer telling investors to stay away from the AI infrastructure trade. In a new note, analysts led by Ohsung Kwon raised the firm's view on US AI infrastructure to neutral from negative.
The change follows a deep selloff. Semiconductor shares trade about 38% below their June highs, and the multiples investors pay for them have compressed. At current prices, the analysts said, valuations imply earnings growth of only about 8% a year.
A compressed multiple means investors now pay less for each dollar of expected profit. That can happen even while earnings keep rising, which is why a stock can fall while its business improves.
Politics Adds a New Worry to the AI Spending Debate
Democratic wins in the midterm elections, including in states that oppose new data centers, fueled concerns about regulation. A stricter permitting climate could slow construction and raise its cost, which would cut into the spending that has fed AI company revenue.
The selloff has erased about $3 trillion from the S&P 500. Readers following the pullback can find the names analysts like most in our list of oversold AI stocks with 50%-plus upside. Kwon and his team said the risk-reward is now reasonable after the drop.
Why 2028 Worries Analysts More Than 2027
AI spending added about 8 percentage points to S&P 500 earnings growth over the past year. The Wells Fargo analysts wrote that "The tailwind is expected to continue in 2027," and that it largely disappears in 2028 as spending growth slows and depreciation costs rise.
Depreciation explains much of the concern. Companies spread the cost of data centers and chips over several years, so those charges keep landing on income statements even after the buying slows. Those charges are real expenses even though the cash left the company earlier. Profit growth then shrinks, just as the spending that lifted it fades. Analysts build their forecasts from spending levels, so a plateau in budgets changes the math quickly.
The bigger risk, the analysts said, is a downturn in earnings per share once capital spending peaks. They also pointed to extra supply arriving in 2028 that prices do not yet reflect. For investors, the question is how much of that is already in share prices after the drop.
Companies still growing quickly through the selloff are the subject of our roundup of the fastest-growing AI stocks. The Wells Fargo shift is a move from caution to a neutral stance, not a call that the selloff is over.

Wall Street had its worst day since April 2025 last Thursday. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%, the S&P 500 dropped 4.4%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2%.
Two worries drove the selling. Investors doubt that heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and candidates who ran against data center expansion won races in Texas and Georgia in the midterm elections. Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, told Reuters that chip stocks are a volatile, cyclical group in which "when sentiment shifts, the reactions are intense." Hedge funds, he added, had been selling for weeks.
Why a Wide Moat Matters When Sentiment Turns
A rout like that tests which businesses can protect their profits when investors lose their nerve. An economic moat is a company's lasting edge over its rivals, the kind that guards its market share and earnings.
Moats come in several forms. A company can be the low-cost producer, own a brand that lets it charge more, or hold patents and licenses that keep copycats out. Scale helps, because large producers spread their costs over more units. High switching costs make customers think twice before moving to a rival. What matters most is how long the advantage lasts and how much it depends on the people running the company.
Stocks have bounced since. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq each climbed more than 1% on Wednesday, and the semiconductor index jumped 7%. Equities have whipsawed all week, though, as worries about slower data center deployment and higher interest rates compete with the urge to buy the dip, Reuters reported.
Brokerages including Morgan Stanley and UBS have called the rout overdone. Morgan Stanley said the likely effect is a push-out of some data center projects from 2028 to 2029, not a derailing of the spending boom. Goldman Sachs estimates that about 45% of planned US data center capacity faces possible restrictions. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s Chief Information Officer, said the potential significance for the US of the recent supermarket freezer hacks in Europe dawned on her abruptly when she first read about them.
“Holy cow! What else uses refrigeration?” she recalled of her immediate reaction, in an interview with Bloomberg News.
Davies described the freezer hacks as “a wake-up call for society,” and she rattled off other vital functions that could be impacted by them, including at military bases: blood banks, plasma and organ donation, manufacturing and transportation of food. She portrayed cyberattacks against so-called operational technology — the software and hardware used for industrial processes and critical infrastructure — as surprisingly easy hacks that have a real-life physical impact, as if an attack is “reaching through digital wires and touching you.”
France this week blamed Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps for attacks on refrigeration units at more than 700 stores that resulted in spoiled food during October and November. Blood banks in France were also affected in early November incidents, although officials said no blood was spoiled thanks to early-warning systems.
Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot vowed to seek sanctions and other unspecified measures. Iran has denied responsibility.
Six US military installations have also acknowledged in public statements that freezers at their commissaries, which sell discounted food to soldiers and their families, went out simultaneously during August. However, they haven’t provided a reason for the outages. Davies said she couldn’t comment on the incidents affecting US military facilities.
The Army Criminal Investigation Division has said it’s working with other investigators to determine the full extent of what occurred.
A Defense Department official said the Pentagon doesn’t comment on intelligence-related matters as a matter of practice and referred a reporter to the official French government statement attributing responsibility to Iran.
Along with one other senior Pentagon official, Davies is responsible for safeguarding US defense critical infrastructure on which the military system relies. Hacks against such technology underline the importance of boosting operational technology security – safeguarding physical equipment that may be connected to the internet, she said.
Davies described OT hacks against the military as “a real threat vector.” “Think about the Navy, and all of the ships and the submarines, and the airplanes, and the software platforms that actually run the way in which a plane would be operating,” she said of the potential hacking threat.
The US military, which employs about 3 million people, also relies on blood banks to treat wounded military personnel, in addition to civilian infrastructure for power, water and fuel systems that are susceptible to attacks against internet-connected machinery. A group of nonprofits sued OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX’s AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google on Thursday, seeking to block the further development of the most advanced AI models over concerns, voiced by the companies’ own leaders, that the technology could pose a threat to humanity.
The nonprofits, which focus on tech accountability and include the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and Heat Initiative, sued in San Francisco, saying California’s laws against unfair business practices provide the grounds for a court order barring the companies from further development of products like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude.
The lawsuit cites comments from company leaders, like Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, and Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive, about AI’s potential to cause the destruction of civilization. It also describes recent incidents where models have escaped testing environments and autonomously attacked government websites.
“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the lawsuit says. “Nor is any industry granted the right to self-regulate the development of such dangerous products.”
The lawsuit accuses the companies of engaging in business practices that create a public nuisance, or harm to public health and enjoyment, pointing to both past incidents and the potential for future harm.
A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. Representatives of the other companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
OTHER LAWSUITS SEEK TO BAR DEVELOPMENT
While the Trump administration has so far declined to pursue large-scale AI regulation over fears it could harm the country’s ability to compete with China, states and private entities have sought to use lawsuits to force the companies to make changes.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in June, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, saying it has harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users. In September, Florida asked the judge overseeing the lawsuit to bar OpenAI from developing new artificial intelligence models without outside oversight. That motion remains pending, according to court records.
After Florida’s filing, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had paused training its most capable models and would not resume until they have additional safeguards in place.
“Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI, and we’re committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company,” Pusateri said.
Separately, a group of eight states sued OpenAI last month in courts across the country alleging ChatGPT has coached its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others. OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment after the filing.
The states’ lawsuits seek financial penalties, as well as an order barring the company from developing self-improving AI models unless it can ensure those models are aligned with human values.
(Reporting by Diana Novak Jones in Chicago; Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Matthew Lewis)

Billion-dollar wildfires in the US have become more than five times as frequent and 10 times as costly over the past two decades, according to a new analysis of the nation’s most destructive fires.
The analysis, from Climate Central, a nonprofit climate research and communications group, looks at individual fires each causing at least $1 billion in damage. Earlier federal estimates combined losses from many fires that occurred during the same wildfire season into a single disaster.
Thirty-one individual wildfires have crossed the $1 billion threshold since 1980, together costing nearly $186 billion and destroying more than 79,500 structures, the analysis finds. An estimated 373 people died in the fires.
The surge reflects both a changing climate and communities’ choices about development, said Adam Smith, the scientist who led the project. “Either way you look at it, the rise in damages relates to human activities,” he said.
From 2007 through 2026, the US experienced 26 billion-dollar wildfires, compared with five during the previous 20 years. Inflation-adjusted losses jumped to $170 billion from $15.6 billion. More than three-quarters of the billion-dollar fires have occurred since 2016, including the $36.3 billion Palisades fire in Los Angeles in 2025 and the $6 billion Lahaina fire in Hawaii in 2023.
Burned cars and homes in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire in Lahaina, Hawaii on 2023. Photographer: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
Climate change is contributing to conditions that increase the likelihood that fires ignite and spread, Smith said. At the same time, increasingly valuable real estate and rising reconstruction costs in areas where communities meet wildlands mean there is more to lose when fires occur.
California dominates the tally, accounting for 23 of the 31 billion-dollar fires and $167 billion of the losses. The others struck in Hawaii, Colorado, Oregon, New Mexico, Tennessee, Texas and Washington.
The analysis changes the way the economic toll of wildfires is measured, looking at fires separately instead of combining all the fires during one season into a single collective disaster. The change produces a more detailed picture but also a lower overall price tag. Under the previous approach, wildfire losses totaled $221 billion, compared with about $186 billion using the new one. The older method included losses from many smaller fires that don’t individually meet the $1 billion threshold.
For decades, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) maintained the US Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database, tracking the nation’s most expensive hurricanes, floods, droughts, wildfires and other events.
NOAA discontinued the project in 2025. Climate Central began operating the database that October, with Smith, who had spent 15 years as lead scientist for the NOAA project, continuing to helm the research.
Climate Central’s goal was to continue the federal dataset, Smith said, expanding the detail available on wildfires while retaining the methodology for assessing other types of disasters. Next year, the group plans to go further, identifying individual fires that caused at least $100 million in damage going back to 1980.
Including the newly separated wildfire events, Climate Central counts 453 billion-dollar US weather and climate disasters since 1980, with total losses of $3.2 trillion.

The driver of a minivan that crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station, killing three women and critically injuring two more, was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence and three counts of murder, police said.
Authorities said the driver was able to talk but appeared to be in shock after Tuesday’s crash, which hit pedestrians and food vendors at a busy intersection in the North Hollywood neighborhood during the height of the evening commute.
Police identified the driver as Ihor Demianenko, 61, who lives in the Valley Village neighborhood. Demianenko was booked early Wednesday and his bail was set at a little over $6 million, records show. He was treated for minor injuries at a hospital, police said.
It wasn’t immediately clear if Demianenko had a lawyer who might speak on his behalf. In California, drivers under the influence of drugs or alcohol can be charged with murder under certain circumstances.
The case had not been presented to the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office as of Wednesday afternoon, spokesperson Venusse Dunn said in an email.
The white Toyota Sienna was traveling at an “unsafe speed” at around 6 p.m. when it veered to the right, ran off the road and collided with a light, Los Angeles police said in a news release Wednesday. It came to rest under a food vendor’s tent.
The force of the collision threw victims in different directions, according to the news release. The driver was trapped in the vehicle until rescuers arrived.
Luis Luna-Guzman was working at a nearby burger stand when he heard a loud boom and saw people on the ground along with food and cups. People started running toward the crash.
Luna-Guzman said he found an injured woman lying near some bike racks, her face, arms and legs bloody. Her eyes were closed as she moaned in pain.
“I told her, ‘Don’t move, help is coming,'” Luna-Guzman said, adding that he saw a woman’s body nearby, while another woman was lying unmoving on the stairs leading to the station.
The three women who died were between the ages of 40 and 60, according to the police news release. Authorities haven’t released their names. The two injured women are in their 50s.
The minivan was still on the sidewalk Tuesday night under the food vendor’s tent, its driver’s-side door open and an air bag deployed. Fire engines and emergency crews worked nearby as a helicopter flew overhead.
Investigators will go through video of the crash frame by frame, Police Chief Jim McDonnell said.
“It will be probably a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here,” he said.
The California Supreme Court ruled in 1981 that drivers who kill someone with a vehicle can be charged with second-degree murder if they are found to have acted with “wantonness and a conscious disregard for life” that could support a finding of implied malice. The court upheld a prosecutor’s decision to file murder charges against a driver who was determined to be legally intoxicated at the time of a fatal crash and drove at high speeds, ran a red light and had a near miss right before.
Thanawala reported from Atlanta.

Missouri to end state-run developmental disability case management
Some disability advocates worry eliminating state positions will remove a necessary layer of oversight of service providers
Support coordinators based in regional offices of the Missouri Department of Mental Health currently provide case management to more than 5,000 individuals with developmental disabilities, mostly in the Kansas City and St. Louis metro areas (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
More than 5,000 Missourians with developmental disabilities who rely on state employees to help them access services will be assigned to outside agencies by the end of 2027, a move that will eliminate 299 state positions.
The Department of Mental Health’s Division of Developmental Disabilities currently provides direct case management to 5,152 people statewide. About 87% of Missourians eligible for services through the division already work with contracted case managers employed by nonprofits or county disability boards.
Support coordinators work with individuals with disabilities and their families to develop and monitor individualized support plans, which identify the person’s needs and goals and, with approval from the division, help them access services, including those funded through Medicaid.
Debra Walker, the department’s director of public affairs, told The Independent the change “will address caseload growth and focus (division) staff time on the division requirements of contract management, quality and compliance.”
The division has sought for years to shift support coordination to outside agencies as the number of Missourians eligible for services through the division has increased, citing the need to keep caseloads manageable. And the move is expected to save the state approximately $3 million annually, Walker said, as spending outpaces revenue and the pandemic-era surplus diminishes.
But some disability advocates worry the transition will disrupt services. Others are concerned that eliminating state-employed case managers could weaken oversight of organizations providing services to people with disabilities and make it more difficult for the state to follow federal rules barring individuals from receiving services from the same entity assessing their eligibility.
An Oct. 28 letter from the division obtained by The Independent tells clients to “continue to meet with your support coordinator as you usually would” and indicates they will be contacted by the division or their new case management provider once their case is transferred.
The transition, which will eliminate 299 state support coordination staff positions, including supervisors, is scheduled to be complete by Dec. 31, 2027.
Current employees will receive preference when applying for openings in the division’s regional offices, but none are guaranteed another position.
Walker said the division has already confirmed contractors’ capacity to serve clients who will be transferred from state support coordinators — 92% of whom are in the Kansas City and St. Louis metro areas.
Larry Opinsky, a disability advocate based in St. Louis County whose daughter uses self-directed services, said he isn’t worried about his family’s transition because he knows how to navigate the state’s disability service system. But for families less familiar with the system, he worries the transition could interrupt or delay services.

Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported.
Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room.
Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room."
But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."
Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s."
"And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate allies, resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday after admitting to an affair following scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly determined to be a Chinese spy.

"Although we expect solid AI investment growth to continue, our forecasts imply that the investment growth impulse — additional AI investment as a share of GDP — will peak in early 2027. From a macro perspective, this should be a manageable event. But it may be a bigger test for markets for three reasons," Goldman Sachs strategist Kamakshya Trivedi said.
"First, the AI impulse has been a much larger contributor to growth in earnings and market value than to growth in GDP," Trivedi explained.
"Second, AI-related equities have taken credit for significant macro productivity gains, especially companies benefiting directly from the infrastructure boom, that have made them more vulnerable to any signs that we are on a less optimistic path," Trivedi added.
Read more: How to protect your money during turmoil, stock market volatility
"Third, the point at which growth rates peak (a "second derivative" turning point) often matters, even if underlying growth rates (the "first derivative") remain healthy. Moving through that peak allows markets to place limits on the upside of an uncertain distribution and, as growth decelerates, the period of positive surprises to expectations often ends too, as we may be starting to see for the AI capex cycle."
Stocks have already been put to the test entering the final weeks of the year.
Market volatility has spiked in recent weeks amid the midterm election aftermath, which will see Democrats take control of the House and Senate in 2027.
High-stakes earnings reports from hyperscalers like Amazon (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) freaked out the market as they highlighted dwindling free cash flow.
The removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia (NVDA) CEO has also triggered a sharp sell-off in hot sectors.
At the same time, macro headwinds have intensified as crude oil prices remain elevated amid geopolitical friction in the Middle East, reigniting fears of sticky headline inflation.

Salesforce (CRM) stock closed on November 12, 2026, 13.1% below its October 22 high. Investors watching the slide want to know whether this is a chance to buy or a fall with further to go. No one can know that yet, but one thing is known for sure: how the stock behaved after its earlier sharp falls since 2010. So what happened to buyers who stepped in after those earlier drops?
Most Salesforce Dip Buyers Were Higher A Year Later
Since 2010, Salesforce stock has fallen more than 20% within 30 trading days on 12 separate occasions. In 8 of the 10 cases at least a year old, shares were higher 252 trading days later, posting a median gain of 32.5% over that year. The other two drops, in February and July 2026, are too recent to judge.
The two instances that lost money lost a lot. Shares bought on the January 5, 2022 dip traded 38% lower a year later. Those bought on the March 11, 2025 dip, the latest one old enough to judge, were down 29%.
Buyers usually sat through a further fall along the way. In the median case, the stock’s lowest close in the following year sat 13.1% below its price on the dip date. Its best price in that year came after a median of 217 calendar days, about seven months.
Is Salesforce’s Business Holding Up Today?
By measures of sales and profit, it is. Over the four fiscal quarters ended July 31, 2026, Salesforce’s revenue grew 11.2%, outpacing the 8.3% recorded over the twelve months before. The company carried a 21.5% operating margin over those twelve months, compared with 19.0% for the S&P 500. Management said on its August 26 call that continued momentum in Slack and Agentforce drove the latest quarter’s growth.
Growth did slow in that quarter, however. Revenue rose 10.8% in fiscal Q2 2027, down from 13.3% in fiscal Q1. Trading at 18.5 times trailing earnings, the stock is priced below the S&P 500’s 21.9 on reported earnings over the past four quarters. Reported earnings can include gains outside the core business, so that gap is a rough guide rather than proof the stock is cheap.
The balance sheet marks a bigger change. Salesforce carried $41.7 billion of total debt on July 31, 2026, compared with $11.2 billion a year earlier. Over the same twelve months, the company bought back $35.1 billion of its own shares, and on October 20 it agreed to acquire Braze in a $5.66 billion deal.
What Must You Believe To Buy Salesforce Now?
Buying now means expecting this fall to end like most of Salesforce’s past drops rather than like the two that lost money, in January 2022 and March 2025. You have some grounds for that in the business: sales growth picked up over the past year, and on reported earnings over the past four quarters, the stock’s P/E sits below the market’s, though that measure is only a rough guide. Against that, growth slowed in fiscal Q2 2027, and the company now carries far more debt than it did a year ago.

It was a hot summer afternoon on Cold Soil Road, and I had just finished the “First Speed Run,” a guided run in the Nike Run Club app. It included eight one-minute intervals interspersed with one minute of recovery. The virtual coach of that run prescribed different speeds, including a mile pace which was “fast,” a 10K pace which was “faster, but slower than a mile pace,” and the slowest of the three, a marathon pace. No matter how much I tried, I couldn’t run at different paces. Over the course of my various flirtations, romances, and relationships with running, I’d always seemed to move at only two speeds: run and walk.
Disappointed and discouraged, I checked to see the name of the next guided run, hoping it wouldn’t force me to struggle, yet again, with unrealistic speeds. The name? “Find Your Pace.” Excited about this fortuitous opportunity, I pressed download and started this short workout even though I had just struggled through the previous one.
Fortunately, Coach Cory, who led this particular guided run, never once asked me to check my Fitbit for metrics and pace. Instead, he only referred to the Rate of Perceived Exertion, a metric that has been around for decades, but that I had, to be honest, ignored for all of that time. RPE is a purely subjective scale from 1 to 10. Typically, 1 refers to an effort level similar to sitting on your couch (i.e., no effort at all), and running at a 3 is a warmup effort. On the other end of the spectrum is 10, an all-out sprint, a pace you can’t sustain for more than half a minute.
Coach Cory explained that my effort level, or exertion, correlated to a variety of distances. For example, I should strive to run a 10K at an RPE of 6, a 5K at 7, and one mile at 9.

These were very short intervals, so my breathing and heart rate didn’t rise much. I followed Coach Cory’s instructions back and forth on the same block, and not once did I look at my Fitbit or the app to see how fast I was going, which is what I was instructed to do during my previous runs. During that one short workout, I realized I could create different paces based on my effort rather than trying to “find” different paces for each race distance.

When a training plan listed different goal paces, I couldn’t seem to reach them, but when I ran based on my RPE, I was able to distinguish between different efforts, and those effort levels translated to mile, 5K, and 10K paces.
This run was memorable. It gave me a boost to not give up on myself or my training.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services wrote in a statement that it’s established an “optional hold harmless period” to give state governments more time to update their systems and improve the processes they have in place.
“States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries—at scale and for the long term,” Dan Brillman, director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services, wrote in the statement.
“If the state can use data to show that someone is working or qualifies for an exclusion, that person should not have to track down paperwork to prove it. It’s unclear if Missouri will take additional time to implement the changes.
“The Missouri Department of Social Services is evaluating new guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services offering states an optional hold harmless period for community engagement implementation,” said Baylee Watts, the department’s media director, in a statement to The Independent Friday afternoon.
The state has poured millions of dollars into preparations to implement the federal law, including hiring contractors to process backlogged Medicaid renewals and an overhaul of the online dashboard participants use to apply for Medicaid and SNAP. Once the requirements are enforced, the state will have to verify that most Missourians ages 19-64 covered through Medicaid expansion worked, attended school or volunteered 80 hours a month to enroll or maintain coverage. The state will also be required to check enrollees’ eligibility every six months instead of annually.
There were 330,490 Medicaid enrollees in Missouri’s adult expansion population as of Nov. 6, according to department data.
